title: Private Deployments: VPC & On-Prem Reference, Day-2 Ops, and Upgrade/Rollback Playbook
author: Priya Shah
summary: Comprehensive reference for customers and SREs operating Redwood Private deployments. Covers VPC deployment patterns, on-prem packaging requirements, recommended reference architectures, day-2 operational procedures, and validated upgrade & rollback playbooks. Intended for engineers, solutions, and customer success teams working on private installs.
body:
Overview

This document consolidates operational guidance for Redwood Private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It contains: a) VPC deployment patterns and networking/security requirements, b) canonical reference architectures for common customer topologies, c) on-prem packaging and installation checklist, d) day-2 operations and monitoring runbooks, and e) upgrade and rollback procedures. Use this as the primary reference during onboarding, pre-sales scoping, and support escalations.

Owners and contacts

- Document owner: Priya Shah (eng-private-deployments)
- Primary oncall for installs: eng-sre oncall rotation (see eng-sre/runbooks)
- Solutions engineering contact: Evan Chen
- Customer success escalation: Maya Patel

Audience and prerequisites

- Audience: SREs, infra engineers, customer platform teams, solutions engineers.
- Prereqs: Customer must provide network diagrams, IP blocks, KMS/HSM access details (if requested), and hardware inventory for on-prem installs. See "Customer requirements library" section for the complete list.

1) VPC Deployment Guide

Goal: Provide a secure, low-latency integration pattern for customers who run Redwood Private inside their cloud VPC with a customer-owned data plane and either a Redwood control plane or customer-hosted control plane.

Supported cloud models

- Customer VPC with Redwood-managed control plane (cross-account peering / PrivateLink depending on cloud)
- Fully customer-managed VPC and control plane (airgapped / private control plane option)

Network topology recommendations

- Minimum subnets: management (control), compute (inference), storage (object/block), bastion (admin).
- AZ distribution: Spread worker pools across 3 AZs for HA where available.
- NAT: NAT gateways required for control plane components that need package updates (optional for airgapped installs if packages are preloaded).

Required ports and endpoints (customer side)

| Source | Destination | Port/Proto | Purpose |
|--------|-------------|-----------:|---------|
| Control plane | Worker nodes | 443/TCP | API calls, heartbeats |
| Worker nodes | S3/Blob storage | 443/TCP | Model artifact pulls / checkpoints |
| Worker nodes | Metrics endpoint (push gateway) | 9091/TCP | Metrics (if push model used) |
| Admin bastion | Control plane / Workers | 22/TCP | SSH for troubleshooting (restricted by CIDR) |
| Control plane | KMS/HSM | 443/TCP | Key encrypt/decrypt operations |

Security controls and IAM

- Principle of least privilege for any roles used to access customer storage and KMS. Provide example IAM policies in the onboarding package.
- Use mutual TLS for control plane <-> worker communication where supported. Certificate management is handled by Redwood by default; for restricted installs we support customer-supplied certificates via the on-prem packaging bundle.

PrivateLink / Peering guidance

- Prefer PrivateLink for hosted control plane integrations when available; it reduces blast radius and simplifies routing.
- For cross-account peering, ensure route table entries in all worker subnets point to the peering connection and update security groups to allow worker <-> control plane traffic.

2) Reference Architectures

This section shows canonical architectures based on expected scale and compliance posture. Each architecture includes components, SLO mappings, and operational notes.

A. Small / Proof-of-Concept (PoC)

- Components: single control plane replica, 2 worker nodes (GPU optional), single AZ, object storage.
- Use case: engineering validation, non-prod testing.
- Recommended SLOs: latency SLOs relaxed (95% < 500ms for short jobs), availability 99%.

B. Production, Multi-AZ (Recommended)

- Components: Highly available control plane (3 replicas), worker pools in 3 AZs, model storage replicated across zones, autoscaler, metrics and logging pipeline (Prometheus + Loki + Cortex/Thanos).
- Networking: private subnets for workers, NAT for egress, private endpoint for control plane.
- SLOs: 99.95% availability for control plane endpoints; inference p95 latency target depends on model class (documented per-customer during onboarding).
- Operational notes: set admission controllers to limit resource overcommit on worker nodes to preserve latency consistency.

C. Air-gapped / Regulated (Restricted Data)

- Components: fully customer-managed control plane, pre-staged artifacts, no external network egress except to approved management CIDRs, HSM/KMS integration on customer network.
- Packaging: full on-prem distribution and offline installer bundle.

3) On-Prem Packaging and Installation Checklist

Supported packaging formats

- Debian (.deb) and RPM (.rpm) packages for server components
- Docker images and Helm charts for Kubernetes deployments
- OVA for customers using VMware vSphere (packaged images)

Minimum hardware profile (per worker node)

| Component | Minimum | Recommended |
|----------|---------:|------------:|
| CPU | 8 vCPU | 32 vCPU |
| RAM | 32 GB | 128 GB |
| GPU | 1x T4 (for small) | 1-8x A10/A100/Tesla depending on throughput |
| Disk | 200 GB SSD | NVMe 1-2 TB |

Installation checklist (pre-install)

1. Confirm customer network diagram and IP ranges.
2. Validate KMS/HSM access: test a sample encryption/decryption key exchange.
3. Confirm storage buckets and credential types (IAM role, signed keys).
4. Verify time sync (NTP) across hosts.
5. Confirm DNS resolution for control plane endpoints and valid TLS certs.
6. Provide preflight script and run against target environment; obtain logs.

Installation steps (high level)

1. Stage packages/artifacts to customer package repository or local registry.
2. Apply base OS hardening and kernel tuning (sysctl) as documented in the packaging guide.
3. Install control plane components and apply initial config (secrets, certs, storage endpoints).
4. Bootstrap worker pools and register to the control plane.
5. Run smoke tests: health endpoints, simple inference job, model pull test, and metrics ingestion test.
6. Hand off runbook and monitoring dashboards to customer SRE.

4) Day-2 Operations (Monitoring, Scaling, and Troubleshooting)

Monitoring and observability

- Required metrics: control plane health (heartbeat), queue depth, per-worker GPU utilization, per-model latency p50/p95/p99, token throughput, model pull errors, disk utilization, and KMS error counts.
- Recommended stack: Prometheus (metrics), Grafana (dashboards), Loki (logs), Cortex/Thanos (long retention), and an alerting engine (PagerDuty integration).

Key dashboards to create

- Cluster overview: node count, CPU/GPU utilization, disk, pod restarts.
- Control plane health: replicas, API latency, failed requests.
- Model performance: per-model latency distributions, error rates, request size histogram.
- Cost/throughput: tokens/sec and estimated cost per 1k tokens by model class.

Common operational procedures

- Scale up/down worker pools:
  1. Verify current utilization and queue depth.
  2. Increase pool desired count by 10-20% for quick experiments.
  3. Observe pod startup times and GPU readiness; re-adjust autoscaler thresholds if necessary.
- Recovering a hung worker:
  1. Drain node from scheduler.
  2. Capture /var/log/redwood and runtime traces.
  3. Restart runtime process and re-register node.
  4. If instability persists, reprovision node from template.
- Addressing model pull failures:
  1. Check storage credentials and endpoint accessibility.
  2. Confirm artifact checksum and size.
  3. If transient, requeue the pull; if persistent, escalate to solutions engineering.

Operational SLOs & alert thresholds (examples)

- Control plane 5xx rate > 0.5% for 5m -> P1 alert.
- Model load failure rate > 1% for 10m -> P1 alert.
- GPU OOM events > 3 in 1h -> P2 alert.
- Disk usage > 85% on any worker -> P2 alert.

5) Upgrade and Rollback Procedures

Upgrade strategy and risks

- We recommend a canary first upgrade followed by a rolling upgrade. The canonical approach is: canary control plane instance(s) -> canary worker pool -> gradual rollout across AZs.
- Risk categories: incompatibility between runtime and model artifacts, driver/kernel mismatches for GPU, and config drift. Verify that the upgrade artifacts include the exact runtime, driver and kernel compatibility matrix.

Pre-upgrade checklist

1. Validate backup: control plane metadata snapshot and storage manifest.
2. Confirm tested rollback artifact is available in local registry.
3. Verify health baseline (pre-upgrade metrics) for comparison.
4. Inform customers (scheduled window) and pause any long-running batch jobs.

Canary upgrade steps (control plane)

1. Deploy upgraded control plane replica into a canary namespace or node pool.
2. Run smoke tests (API health, authentication, basic inference flows).
3. Run integration tests with a small percentage (1-5%) of production traffic.
4. Monitor error rates and latency for 15-30 minutes. If metrics degrade beyond thresholds, initiate rollback.

Rolling upgrade (workers)

1. Add a canary worker pool with the new image; direct small traffic.
2. After canary validation, drain a subset of nodes in each AZ and reprovision with the new image.
3. Do not modify scheduling or autoscaler thresholds during the rolling window unless required.
4. Monitor model load success rate, GPU temps, and latencies closely.

Rollback procedure (fast path)

1. If canary signals failure, stop the rollout and scale up the previous version for the affected component.
2. For control plane rollback: revert to the previous replica set and reapply previous config. Wait for quorum and re-validate the API.
3. For worker rollback: cordon new nodes, reintroduce previous image nodes, and move workloads back.
4. Validate data integrity and run post-rollback smoke tests.

Post-upgrade verification

- Compare pre/post baselines for p95 latency, error rate, and model load success. If any regression > 10% persists, create a regression ticket and engage runtime engineering for triage.

6) Customer Requirements Library (Onboarding checklist and templates)

Provide this checklist to customer engineering teams during scoping. Items marked (mandatory) must be provided before scheduling a private install.

Mandatory items (pre-install)

- Signed security & compliance questionnaire (mandatory)
- Network diagram and address ranges (CIDR blocks) (mandatory)
- Accounts and roles for object storage, or signed short-lived credentials (mandatory)
- KMS/HSM access details and test key (mandatory for encrypted deployments)
- SSH bastion access CIDR and admin contacts (mandatory)
- Inventory of GPU hardware and driver versions (mandatory for on-prem)

Optional / recommended items

- Monitoring endpoints and existing Grafana dashboards for integration
- Existing certificate authority details for mutual TLS
- Pre-approved maintenance windows and change management process

Templates included in the onboarding package

- IAM policy snippets for S3/Blob access (JSON)
- Example security questionnaire and SOC/compliance mappings (PDF)
- Preflight validation script (.sh) and sample outputs
- Helm values.yml example for a 3-AZ production deployment

Appendices

A. Troubleshooting quick commands

- Check health endpoints: curl -fsS https://control-plane.example.internal/health
- List worker pods: kubectl get pods -n redwood-workers -o wide
- Show runtime logs: journalctl -u redwood-runtime -n 500

B. Kernel and driver compatibility notes

- GPU driver minimum supported: NVIDIA 525.x (subject to change per model); consult packaging release notes for exact matrix.
- CUDA versions and supported runtimes are included in each release bundle.

C. Audit & Compliance handoff checklist

- Ensure audit logging is enabled and logs retained per customer policy (default 90 days configurable).
- Provide signed attestation for package integrity and supply chain notices for the installed bundle.

Status and followups

This document is published and will be reviewed quarterly. Owners must ensure compatibility matrices in the Appendices are kept in sync with release notes. For major architecture changes or new cloud integrations, open an ADR under confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records.
